newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Gulf Arab states seek more jobs for nationals.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arab states seek more jobs for nationals.

text.p: Gulf Arab labour ministers began two days of talks in Bahrain on Monday with calls to find more jobs for their citizens and to integrate and coordinate social affairs and work in their countries.

"The council is required to follow up resolutions...to find job opportunities for the citizens, facilitate their employment and their movement between GCC states," the secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), Jameel Hujilan, said.
"Providing job opportunities needs our collective efforts," he said.

The GCC states -- Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Qatar, United Arab Emirates and Kuwait -- have begun a drive to find more jobs for their citizens in an attempt to reduce alliance on millions of expatriates who help them run their economies.
Foreigners comprise one-third of Saudi Arabia's estimated 18 million population. In the United Arab Emirates, three out of four people are expatriates.
Some Gulf Arab states have deported Asian labourers, mostly from the Indian subcontinent, found to be working illegally.
A Gulf official said last month foreign workers accounted for more than 80 percent, and in some cases reached 90 percent, of the labourers working in GCC manufacturing industries.

Abdul-Rahman al-Jaafari, secretary-general of the Gulf Organisation for Industrial Consulting, said the GCC needed to invest at least $1.5 billion a year in the manufacturing sector over the next 30 years to keep pace with current labour growth.
Bahrain's Labour and Social Affairs Minister Abdel-Nabi al-Shula said Bahrain was working to find more jobs for its citizens and had taken steps to regulate labour.
He said the island had also embarked on an ambitious training programme with the help of the private sector to find more jobs for Bahrainis to combat rising unemployment.
Bahrain opened its first Employment Services Bureau last August to assist, guide and train jobless Bahrainis. Unemployment in Bahrain has helped fuel anti-government unrest over the last two years.
